title: CASE OF VAREY v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
conclusion: Struck out of the list (friendly settlement)
summary: In the case of Varey v. the United Kingdom, the applicants, who identified as Gypsies by birth and were part of the broader Roma and Traveller communities, brought a complaint against the United Kingdom. Their vulnerability stemmed from the persistent difficulties faced by Roma and Traveller families in securing lawful places to live, particularly due to restrictive planning policies and the lack of authorised caravan sites. The applicants, having lived nomadically in the Stafford area, purchased land that had historically been used by Gypsies and sought planning permission to establish a residential caravan site. Despite repeated applications and appeals between 1988 and 1997, the local council and the Secretary of State consistently refused permission, citing Green Belt development policies. The applicants faced enforcement notices, criminal convictions, fines, and ultimately, the threat of imprisonment and forced eviction, leaving them with no lawful alternative accommodation. The case raised issues under Articles 6 (right to a fair hearing), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, before a final judgment, the parties reached a friendly settlement, and the European Court of Human Rights struck the case out of its list. This case highlights the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in accessing secure housing in the United Kingdom, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation and legal obstacles across Europe.
